_comment: 🎛️ Contribution of the repo coordinator owner. Every entry is resolved from the repository's own node_modules or from the Node standard library, imported only from 🧪️tests/**/🟦️.ts, and never reachable from any implementation. Ids are owner-scoped, so this survey never reuses another owner's node:crypto entry.

oracles.rationale: 🔏️ Both implementations hand-roll SHA-256 — the Rust crate borrows the events crate's `Sha256`, the Go package uses `crypto/sha256` — and the checksum formula is frozen in 🧫️fixtures/🧬️g3-event-schema.json as text, not as code. Comparing the two implementations only to each other would prove that one reading of that sentence was transcribed twice. `node:crypto` reaches OpenSSL, an independent FIPS 180-4 implementation, and decides the envelope checksum and the canonical line from outside this repository.

noOracleDecisions.rationale: 🚧️ No third party implements this repository's staged-append recovery contract — write `.next`, publish a `.stage` record naming both checksums, move the live log aside to `.backup`, replace it, then drop every artifact; on reopen decide from the stage record which of the three files is the last valid log. A conforming SHA-256 tool judges the digests inside that record but has no opinion on the decision itself. The digests are held by `node-crypto-repo-coordinator`; the recovery half is held by the independently written Go and Rust implementations agreeing, plus each implementation's own unit tests over every phase.

🚧️ The fault plan injects a failure at the Nth durable metadata mutation of one append. No third-party library exposes that seam, and no reference implementation of it exists; both implementations expose the same fixture-driven `arm fault at N` port precisely so the same plan can be replayed against each. Confidence comes from Go and Rust producing the same committed-prefix answer for every index in the plan.

🚧️ The route table, the status codes and the response bodies are this repository's own contract, not a standard any third party implements — an HTTP client can transport the requests but cannot say what `/diff/ingest` ought to answer. A TypeScript oracle would also have to start a Go and a Rust server to have anything to judge, which the harness forbids for the oracle role (it must not compile the subject). The judgement is therefore pairwise equivalence between the two independently written servers, each started by its own adapter on an ephemeral port and driven by the same committed request fixture.
